evidence.label: Scale and conformal symmetry in four-dimensional operational quantum field theory

headline: Claims that scale symmetry forces local conformal symmetry for a broad class of four-dimensional quantum field theories.
scope: Unitary, positive-energy quantum field theories in four spacetime dimensions with a discrete spectrum of scaling dimensions and a bounded local net.
plain: A theory has scale symmetry when it looks the same after every length is stretched by one factor. Conformal symmetry is stronger: the theory also looks the same under maps that stretch by different amounts at different points. Physicists have long asked whether the first forces the second in four dimensions. This paper claims to prove it does, for a class of theories defined by explicit technical conditions. The conclusion is local and does not build a global conformal action.
doesNot: This does not cover every four-dimensional theory, and it does not build a global conformal action on the whole local net.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Joseph Polchinski, scale implies conformal symmetry in two dimensions under suitable hypotheses
scorecard.significanceWhy: Whether scale symmetry implies conformal symmetry in four dimensions is a long-standing question in quantum field theory.

explanation:
Start with the simplest example, a free massless field φ in four-dimensional spacetime. Its energy and momentum are packed into a table of numbers called the stress tensor, T. Add up the table's diagonal with the spacetime signs and you get its trace. For this field the trace equals −(∂φ)², minus the squared gradient of φ. Treat φ as an ordinary function to see the numbers. Take φ = t·x, time times one space coordinate, which solves the wave equation. Its squared gradient is x² − t². At t = 1 and x = 2 that is 3, so the trace is −3.

Scale symmetry means the theory looks the same after every length is stretched by one factor. Conformal symmetry also allows maps that stretch by different amounts at different points. A theory with conformal symmetry needs a stress tensor with zero trace. Here the trace is −3, not zero. But the trace is a total second derivative. The wave operator □ of Q = φ² is 2x² − 2t², which is 6 at our point. So the trace equals □(−Q/2), and −6/2 = −3. In the paper's words, the needed scalar is already present, L = −Q/2[1]. Adding a correction built from Q gives a new tensor. Its trace is −3 + (4·6 − 6)/6 = 0. This fix is called an improvement, and it leaves the energy and momentum unchanged.

The general question is whether such a scalar always exists. In two dimensions, Zamolodchikov's c-theorem and Polchinski's 1988 argument settled it under suitable hypotheses[2]. In four dimensions, consistency conditions give a perturbative answer, valid only at weak coupling. The positivity those arguments need is not established at arbitrary coupling[3]. The obstacle is to find the scalar L inside the theory's own fields. Dividing the trace by a wave operator gives a candidate, but it may not be a genuine local field.

This paper claims that scale symmetry implies local conformal symmetry for a class of four-dimensional theories[4]. The theories must be unitary, have positive energy and a vacuum that looks the same at every scale. Their scaling dimensions must form a discrete list bounded below. The paper claims a physical scalar field L of dimension two exists[5]. With it, the stress tensor gets a symmetric, conserved, traceless improvement with unchanged translation and Lorentz charges[6]. No scattering states or assumed crossing relation enter the argument[7]. The result is local. Building a global conformal action on the whole local net remains a separate question[8].

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The argument is a long chain of operator estimates in an abstract framework. Its hypotheses are explicit, and checking that a given interacting theory meets them is a separate task. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. It covers only theories meeting explicit technical conditions and gives a local result. There is no Lean check and no published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: A table of numbers at each point that records the density and flow of energy and momentum.
The sum of the stress tensor's diagonal entries, with the signs that spacetime uses.
The theory looks the same after every length is stretched by the same factor.
The theory looks the same under maps that stretch by different amounts at different points while keeping angles.
A correction added to the stress tensor that leaves the total energy, momentum and angular momentum unchanged.
The second time derivative minus the sum of the second space derivatives.
An assignment of an algebra of measurements to each bounded region of spacetime.
